vignette:
She is 49, a South Eastern Asian woman who now works in IT support, the person colleagues call when the printer jams, the VPN drops, or someone cannot get back into an account. She is calm on the phone and careful with her words. People at work know her as reliable, private, and unusually good in a crisis. What they do not see is how much of her life is still organized around an older battlefield.

She grows up in a place where war is not an abstraction but weather, something that settles over daily life and changes what is possible. By the time she is a young woman, combat has become woven into ordinary routines: listening before opening a door, scanning roads, memorizing exits, noticing the difference between distant thunder and artillery. During the worst period, she is caught in repeated fighting near her community. She sees bodies in places where children should be playing. She learns to go still when planes pass overhead. Once, during an attack, she spends hours pressed into a cramped shelter with other civilians, breathing dust and sweat, certain the walls will come down. A man beside her bleeds and calls for his mother until he goes quiet. She remembers the smell more than the sound.

After that, fear no longer comes and goes. It settles inside her. Even when she is technically safe, her body behaves as if safety is temporary and probably false. She startles at bangs, drops to a crouch before she can think, and feels ashamed when she realizes where she is. At night she dreams in fragments: concrete, smoke, a child’s shoe, hands over her ears. She wakes with her heart racing and has to turn on all the lights to remind herself which country and which year she is in.

She eventually leaves and builds a life elsewhere. From the outside, it looks like a steady climb. She learns new systems, improves her English, marries, finds work, raises herself into a dependable adult life. She is drawn to IT support partly because computers make sense to her in a way people often do not. Problems have causes. Causes can be traced. If one approach fails, there is usually another. She likes restoring order after disruption. She likes being the person who can stay composed when others are flustered.

But the old alarms remain active beneath that competence. In open-plan offices, she chooses the desk with the clearest line to the exit. She notices everyone who enters the room. If a coworker drops a box behind her, a jolt runs through her whole body before she can mask it with a tight smile. During mandatory emergency drills, she feels her chest constrict and her thoughts narrow. She knows it is a drill; she also knows that her hands are shaking too hard to use her keycard. Once, when a fire alarm starts unexpectedly, she leaves the building quickly and efficiently, then keeps walking until she is three blocks away, crying in anger at herself because she cannot will her body to calm down.

Her marriage does not survive her distance. She says her ex-husband used to tell her she was never fully in the room. She does not disagree. She loves in a watchful way, with duty and vigilance, but closeness is hard because closeness means letting down her guard. She sleeps lightly, often on the edge of the bed, and wakes irritated if someone touches her unexpectedly. When he asks about her past, she gives him edited versions, then feels alone when he does not understand her.

In the present, her world is narrow but functional. She goes to work, pays bills, calls her relatives, cooks familiar foods, and avoids crowded celebrations where fireworks or loud music might surprise her. News from overseas can undo an entire evening. Certain smells—diesel, damp concrete, something metallic in the air after rain—pull her backward so suddenly that for a few seconds she is no longer in a parking garage or train station but in the shelter again, waiting for impact. She hates those moments most, the way time folds and her body believes the past over the evidence of the present.

She is tired of being on guard and yet does not know how to stop. She checks locks more than once before bed. She keeps extra batteries, bottled water, copies of documents, and a packed bag in the closet, not because she expects disaster exactly, but because not preparing feels reckless. She rarely tells anyone how much effort ordinary life requires. At work she resets passwords and troubleshoots frozen screens while monitoring the hum of the fluorescent lights, the foot traffic in the hall, the pitch of voices around her. She can solve three technical problems at once, but if a helicopter passes low overhead, her concentration disappears and her skin goes cold.

She says the war ended years ago, and she knows that is true in the way facts are true. But inside her, it has never fully stopped.
